correct_citation: White, T. G., Kim, J. S., Kingston, H. C., & Foster, L. (2014). Replicating the effects of a teacher-scaffolded voluntary summer reading program: The role of poverty. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(1), 5-30. doi:10.1002/rrq.62

outcome: Reading (test not named in abstract)

correct_citation: Kim, J. S., Guryan, J., White, T. G., Quinn, D. M., Capotosto, L., & Kingston, H. C. (2016). Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 9(sup1), 1-22. doi:10.1080/19345747.2016.1164780

correct_citation: Guryan, J., Kim, J. S., & Quinn, D. M. (2014). Does reading during the summer build reading skills? Evidence from a randomized experiment in 463 classrooms. NBER Working Paper 20689 (ERIC ED619516, dated 2022).

correct_citation: Kim, J. S., & White, T. G. (2008). Scaffolding voluntary summer reading for children in grades 3 to 5: An experimental study. Scientific Studies of Reading, 12(1), 1-23.

correct_citation: Bus, A. G., Shang, Y., & Roskos, K. (2024). Building a stronger case for independent reading at school. AERA Open, 10. doi:10.1177/23328584241267843

correct_citation: Erbeli, F., & Rice, M. (2022). Examining the effects of silent independent reading on reading outcomes: A narrative synthesis review from 2000 to 2020. Reading & Writing Quarterly, 38(3), 253-271. doi:10.1080/10573569.2021.1944830

correct_citation: Somers, M.-A., Welbeck, R., Grossman, J. B., & Gooden, S. (2015). An analysis of the effects of an academic summer program for middle school students. MDRC.

correct_citation: Pyne, J., Messner, E., & Dee, T. S. (2023). The dynamic effects of a summer learning program on behavioral engagement in school. Education Finance and Policy, 18(2). doi:10.1162/edfp_a_00368 (working paper: CEPA WP 20-10, ERIC ED609963)

correct_citation: Chaplin, D., & Capizzano, J. (2006). Impacts of a summer learning program: A random assignment study of Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL). Urban Institute.

correct_citation: Schueler, B. E., & Larned, K. E. (2025). Interscholastic policy debate promotes critical thinking and college-going: Evidence from Boston Public Schools. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. doi:10.3102/01623737231200234

correct_citation: Anderson, S., & Mezuk, B. (2012). Participating in a policy debate program and academic achievement among at-risk adolescents in an urban public school district: 1997-2007. Journal of Adolescence, 35(5), 1225-1235.

note: Method is regression (not matching). Abstract does not say whether 8th-grade achievement was a covariate or only part of the risk index. Associational design.

correct_citation: Kraft, M. A. (2015). How to make additional time matter: Integrating individualized tutorials into an extended day. Education Finance and Policy, 10(1), 81-116.

note: Abstract says 'tenth-grade exams' and does not name MCAS.

correct_citation: Dietrichson, J., Filges, T., Klokker, R. H., Viinholt, B. C. A., Bog, M., & Jensen, U. H. (2020). excerpt: The average effect size for short-run outcomes was positive and statistically significant (weighted average effect size [ES] = 0.22, 95% CI = [0.148, 0.284]).

correct_citation: Nakamoto, J., Sobolew-Shubin, S., & Orland, M. (2015). The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, an Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student impact findings from years 1, 2, and 3. WestEd.

correct_citation: Page, M. A., Snyder, C., & Dowell, K. (2024). The Lyceum impact evaluation report. The Evaluation Group for Guilford County Schools.

note: The report names both EIR and the Assistance for Arts Education Development and Dissemination (AAEDD) grant (award U351D180019). Authors caution about small samples.

correct_citation: Foster, E. M., & Jenkins, J. V. M. (2017). Does participation in music and performing arts influence child development? American Educational Research Journal, 54(3), 399-443.

population_location: Large, nationally representative sample (dataset not named in abstract)

note: Direction and design confirmed. 'ECLS-K' is not confirmed, and outcomes in early adulthood suggest a different longitudinal dataset. Named outcomes are GPA, self-esteem and college attendance, not test scores. Full text paywalled.

correct_citation: Walker, E., Tabone, C., & Weltsek, G. (2011). When achievement data meet drama and arts integration. Language Arts, 88(5), 365-372.

outcome: State assessment pass rates in language arts and math; sustained 8th-grade proficiency
effect_as_reported: Odds of passing language arts +77%, math +42%; 78% vs 69% 8th-grade LA proficiency for exited students

note: Effects confirmed. Whether the analysis accounted for school clustering (8 schools) cannot be determined from the abstract; full text paywalled.

correct_citation: Elpus, K. (2013). Is it the music or is it selection bias? A nationwide analysis of music and non-music students' SAT scores. Journal of Research in Music Education, 61(2), 175-194.

population_location: ELS:2002 restricted-use, nationally representative (N = 15,630), US class of 2004
outcome: SAT scores (replicated with another standardized math test)

excerpt: Results indicated that music students did not outperform non-music students on the SAT once these systematic differences had been statistically controlled.

correct_citation: Durham, R. E. (2018). Baltimore OrchKids: An examination of student outcomes. Baltimore Education Research Consortium.
design: Quasi-experimental propensity score matching (gender, age, race, services, September absence, school characteristics, prior achievement where available) plus regression with matching covariates
population_location: Baltimore City Schools OrchKids OST participants, 2009-10 to 2016-17
outcome: Mobility, attendance, chronic absence, suspension, MSA/PARCC ELA and math proficiency
effect_as_reported: Pre-K-4 starters persisting more than one year: higher attendance, lower chronic absence, fewer suspensions; MSA ELA proficient 65.6% (5-8 yr) vs 30.8% comparison (p<.05); PARCC ELA only marginal (33.3% vs 14.1%, p<.10); 5th-8th starters: no ELA/math differences

note: Baseline equivalence was not fully achieved: the report says significant differences remained after matching for some groups. Analyses are by years of participation, and 1-year participants are included. ELA is positive only for long-term elementary starters on the MSA; PARCC ELA is marginal. Funded by the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra.

correct_citation: Holbrook, H. M., Martin, M., Glik, D., Hudziak, J. J., Copeland, W. E., Lund, C., & Fender, J. G. (2022). Music-based mentoring and academic improvement in high-poverty elementary schools. Journal of Youth Development.

outcome: Smarter Balanced (SBAC) ELA and math scores
effect_as_reported: ELA +26 points (beta = 0.08, p = 0.002); math +17 points (beta = 0.06, p = 0.02); larger for lowest prior achievers
excerpt: HP participation was associated with higher standardized scores for math (+17 points; [beta] = 0.06, p = 0.02) and English language arts (+26 points; [beta] = 0.08, p = 0.002).
note: Journal: Journal of Youth Development (Clemson University Press).

correct_citation: Gorard, S., Siddiqui, N., See, B. H., Smith, E., & White, P. (2017). Children's University: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation.

excerpt: Children ever eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) made 1 additional month's progress in maths, no additional progress in reading

correct_citation: Meredith, J., & Anderson, L. M. (2015). Analysis of the impacts of City Year's Whole School Whole Child model on partner schools' performance. Policy Studies Associates (commissioned by City Year).

note: Title page reads 'Commissioned by City Year'.

correct_citation: Russell, C. A., & Meredith, J. (2019). Literacy learning in drop-in library programs: Evaluation of the Free Library of Philadelphia's LEAP Program. Policy Studies Associates.

correct_citation: Piccinino, K., Pepper, S. K., Salomon, H., Greenfield, S., McClanahan, W., & Robertson-Kraft, C. (2020). Springboard Summer Reading Program evaluation report. Springboard Collaborative with McClanahan Associates and ImpactED.

population_location: Districts incl. Norwalk, ICS, Public Prep, APS, OUSD; comparison analysis uses Public Prep, ICS, OUSD; rising K-4

correct_citation: York, B. N., Loeb, S., & Doss, C. (2019). One step at a time: The effects of an early literacy text-messaging program for parents of preschoolers. Journal of Human Resources, 54(3), 537-566 (NBER WP 20659); Doss, C. J., Fahle, E. M., Loeb, S., & York, B. N. (2018). More than just a nudge. NBER WP 24450.

correct_citation: Chang, A., Mauer, E., Wanzek, J., Kim, S., Scammacca, N., & Swanson, E. (2025). Examining the academic effects of cross-age tutoring: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37. doi:10.1007/s10648-025-09997-z

outcome: Academic outcomes

correct_citation: Zief, S. G., Lauver, S., & Maynard, R. A. (2006). Impacts of after-school programs on student outcomes. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 2(1). doi:10.4073/csr.2006.3

correct_citation: Lester, A. M., Chow, J. C., & Melton, T. N. (2020). Quality is critical for meaningful synthesis of afterschool program effects: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 49(2), 369-382.

correct_citation: Baker, S. K., Kamata, A., Wright, A., Farmer, D. E., & Nippert, R. (2019). Using propensity score matching to estimate treatment effects of afterschool programs on third-grade reading outcomes. Journal of Community Psychology, 47(1), 117-134. doi:10.1002/jcop.22104
design: Propensity score matching
population_location: Students served by community providers' afterschool interventions (location not in abstract)
